## Synopsis: Definition and Scope
- Microsurgery and supermicrosurgery refer to the surgical coaptation of small vessels.
- Usually around 1 mm in diameter or smaller.
- Performed under microscope magnification.
- Not limited to blood vessels; includes tiny nerves and lymphatics.

## Synopsis: Evolution and Tools
- Evolved significantly over the last four decades.
- Started from revascularization and replantation in the 1960s.
- Progressed to free flap surgery.
- Aided by operating microscopes, microinstruments, and ultra-fine sutures.

## Synopsis: Techniques and Challenges
- Most common techniques: end-to-end and end-to-side anastomosis, coupling devices.
- Difficult situations can be overcome:
  - Vessel diameter discrepancy
  - Inadequate vessel length
  - Poor vessel quality

## Synopsis: Impact and Demands
- High success rates make free tissue transfer a first-line option.
- Superior results and high patient satisfaction.
- Mentally and physically demanding.
- Special training is mandatory.

## Synopsis: Success and Future
- Preoperative planning and flawless execution are mandatory.
- Clinical assessment is the gold standard for monitoring.
- Success rates reach 96–98% in developed centers.
- Future directions: supermicrosurgery, free-style free flaps, composite tissue allotransplantation.

## Introduction: Defining Microsurgery
- General term for surgery requiring an operating microscope or high magnification loupes.
- Terms vary by structure:
  - Microvascular surgery (vessels ~1 mm)
  - Microneural surgery
  - Microlymphatic surgery
  - Microtubular surgery

## Introduction: Supramicrosurgery
- An extreme form of microsurgery.
- Refers to anastomoses of vessels around 0.5 mm in diameter (0.3–0.8 mm).
- Common applications:
  - Lymphatic reconstruction
  - Perforator-to-perforator anastomosis / repair
  - Distal digital replantation

## Introduction: Reconstructive Microsurgery
- Utilizes micro- and supramicrosurgical techniques.
- Procedures include revascularization, replantation, auto- or allotransplantation.
- Solves problems from:
  - Traumatic injuries
  - Congenital deformities
  - Tumor ablation

## Introduction: Magnification and Scope
- Some procedures performed under loupe magnification (×2.5–8).
- Especially when vessel diameter is not too small (usually 2–3 mm).
- Scope of practice within plastic surgery remains the most diverse in modern surgery.

## History: Early Vascular Repair Concepts
- Concept of vascular repair first proposed by Paré in 1552.
- First successful brachial artery repair performed in 1759.
- 1897: Murphy reported successful end-to-end anastomosis of the femoral artery by invagination with fine silk.

## History: Alexis Carrel's Breakthrough
- 1902: Alexis Carrel reported a technical breakthrough.
- Introduced the triangulation method for end-to-end vascular anastomoses.
- Collaborated with Guthrie.
- Awarded the Nobel Prize in 1912 for "vascular suture and the transplantation of blood vessels and organs".

## History: The Microscope Era Begins
- 1590: Compound microscope invented by Janssen.
- Late 1800s: Mass-produced by Carl Zeiss for lab research.
- 1921: Carl-Olof Siggesson Nylen (Swedish otologist) first used a modified monocular microscope for animal surgery.
- Later in 1921: Used in a patient with chronic otitis and pseudofistula.

## History: Binocular Microscopes
- 1922: Nylen’s monocular microscope replaced by a binocular microscope.
- Developed by his colleague Gunnar Holmgren.
- 1946: Perritt applied the use of the microscope to ophthalmology.

## History: Modern Microvascular Surgery Starts
- 1960: Vascular surgeons Jacobson and Suarez introduced the diploscope.
- A stereoscopic microscope for simultaneous use by two surgeons.
- Allowed anastomoses of vessels as small as 1 mm in diameter.
- Led to extensive use in peripheral nerve, plastic, and neurosurgery.

## History: First Clinical Replantations
- First clinical application of microvascular surgery was in replantation.
- 1964: Malt and McKhann reported successful replantation of several arms.
- 1965: Konatsu and Tamai performed the first complete thumb replantation using a microscope.

## History: Toe-to-Hand Transfers
- 1966: Young reported a series of second toe-to-hand transfers.
- 1967: Cobbett performed the first successful great toe-to-thumb transfer in a human being.

## History: Early Free Flap Experiments
- 1965: Krizek et al. transplanted experimental flaps based on superficial epigastric vessels in dogs.
- 1971: Antia performed the first clinical free flap (dermolipomatous groin flap for facial defect).
- The flap was complicated by infection and partial necrosis.

## History: First Successful Free Flaps
- 1970: McLean and Buncke performed the omental free flap (first fully successful free flap).
- 1973: Daniel and Taylor reported the transfer of the first groin flap.
- New musculocutaneous flaps were designed next, expanding indications.

## History: Perforator Flaps Emerge
- Late 1980s and 1990s: Research focused on anatomy, physiology, and better donor sites.
- Late 1980s: Cutaneous flaps based on perforator vessels evolved from conventional musculocutaneous flaps.
- Intramuscular dissection preserved function and major vessels.

## History: The True Perforator Flap
- 1989: Koshima and Soeda reported the first true perforator flap.
- The deep inferior epigastric artery perforator (DIEP) flap.
- Next milestone: The free-style flap.
- Allowed harvest based on an audible perforator detected by hand-held Doppler.

## History: Allotransplantation Milestones
- 1998: First successful hand transplantation in Lyon, France.
- January 1999: First successful hand transplantation in Louisville, USA.
- Over 130 patients have received hand/arm transplants worldwide.
- Longest surviving hand/arm transplant is the first US recipient (11 years).

## History: Face Transplantations
- 2005: First partial face transplantation performed in Lyon, France.
- 2010: First total face transplantation performed in Barcelona, Spain.
- More than 45 patients have received full or partial face transplants worldwide.
- Widespread application depends more on immunosuppression than microsurgery advances.

## Tools for Microsurgery
- Evolution of tools allowed progressively smaller vessel anastomoses.
- Alexis Carrel's triangulation technique was the starting point.
- Developments in:
  - Surgical techniques
  - Instrumentation
  - Microsutures
  - Improved optics

## Surgical Microscopes: Basic Sophistication
- Binocular head with adjustable eyepieces.
- Teaching head allows two people to work with magnification.
- Third head available for digital recording.
- Heads independently pivot with separate magnification levels.

## Surgical Microscopes: Controls and Features
- Tilt, focus, and zoom controlled via foot pedal or hand panel.
- Foot pedal keeps hands free but requires coordination.
- Antimicrobial-coated surfaces and internally routed cables.
- Prevents loose wiring from harboring bacteria or getting in the way.

## Surgical Microscopes: Magnification and Optics
- Up to 62× magnifications with instant change.
- Variable working distance (e.g., 10× eyepiece, 200 mm objective lens).
- Some microscopes (Leica, OPMI Pentero) incorporate intraoperative fluorescence tools.
- Invaluable for checking perfusion and precise tumor ablation.

## Surgical Microscopes: Mounting and Usage
- Can be mounted on a stand, table top, or worn on the head.
- Hung on ceiling or wall to conserve floor space.
- Choosing appropriate magnification is crucial:
  - Low (6×–12×): Vessel preparation and suture tying
  - Middle (15×–19×): Suture placement
  - High: Very small vessel anastomosis and inspection

## Box 25.1: Tips for Using Surgical Microscopes
- Familiarize yourself with the microscope.
- Adjust interpupillary distance and diopter correction.
- Use an adjustable seat; sit comfortably with feet flat.
- Upper extremities well supported to minimize fatigue and tremor.
- Focus adjusted at highest magnification before starting.

## Loupes: Overview and Advantages
- Provide magnifications of 2.5×–8×.
- Mounted on glasses or headbands.
- Cost-effective, portable, and offer operator freedom.
- Invaluable for precise dissection and placement of instruments.
- High-magnification loupes can be an effective alternative to microscopes for 1 mm vessels.

## Loupes: Compound (Galilean) Type
- Consist of two magnifying lenses separated by air.
- Higher magnification, greater depth of field, better working distance.
- Drawbacks:
  - Image distortion above 2.5×
  - "Halo" effect at the periphery of the visual field
- Relatively low cost and light weight.

## Loupes: Prismatic Type
- Higher optical quality due to a Schmidt prism.
- Lengthens light path through mirror reflections.
- Improved magnification, wider fields of view, longer depths of field.
- Drawbacks:
  - 30–40% heavier
  - More expensive
  - More easily damaged

## Choosing Loupes: Magnification Guidelines
- 2.5×: Often sufficient for hand surgery and flap harvesting.
- 3.5×–4.5×: Suitable for perforator dissection, thin flaps, or anastomoses.
- Field of view and depth of field decrease with increasing magnification.
- Weight increases; >4.5× tends to be cumbersome and cause neck tension.

## Choosing Loupes: Features and Customization
- Lens design, working angle, and distances must be considered.
- Mounted on glasses or headbands.
- Through-the-lens vs. flip-up or snap-fit types.
- Flip-up permits cheaper changing of magnification and prescriptions.
- Headlights can be supplied for additional lighting.

## Microsurgical Instruments: Essential Features
- Fine tips to spread, hold, or cut delicate tissue and suture.
- Nonreflective surface.
- Comfortable handles that close easily to prevent fatigue.
- Many are spring-loaded; choosing the right spring tension is important.
- Made of heat-hardened stainless steel or antimagnetic titanium.

## Microsurgical Instruments: Maintenance
- Prone to magnetization; store on demagnetized shelves.
- Demagnetize using a coil demagnetizer.
- Available with round or flat handles, 10–18 cm in length.
- Shorter for hand surgery; longer (>18 cm) for free tissue transfer.
- Store in specially designed cases; protect tips with silicone/rubber tubes.

## Microsurgical Scissors
- Spring-loaded with sharp but gently curved blades.
- Slightly rounded tips.
- Can be held closed and used safely as a dissecting probe.
- Straight blades with sharp tips designed for trimming adventitia or cutting stitches.
- In reality, one curved scissor is often adequate for both tasks.

## Needle Holders: Design and Usage
- Spring-loaded, held like pencils, resting on the first web space.
- Handle ideally rounded to roll between fingers.
- Jaws should be thin, gently curved with narrow shoulders.
- Curved style is finer at the tip and suitable for vessel dilatation.
- Unlocking needle holders are preferred to avoid tissue trauma.

## Needle Holders in Supermicrosurgery
- Titanium is preferred for lighter weight.
- Allows order-specific manufacturing to meet operator diversity.
- Maintains flexible and tight grip without needle bending.
- Tips are usually extra delicate for 12-0 and smaller sutures.

## Forceps: Jeweler's Forceps
- Originally designed by the Swiss Dumont factory.
- Flat handle and sharply narrowing tips.
- Tips aligned with a precision of 1/1000 inch.
- Jaws meet evenly over 3 mm when closed with moderate pressure.
- Classified by width of contact surface, narrowness, and configuration.

## Forceps: Types and Usage
- Smooth-tipped are most common; can also be toothed, curved, or angled.
- Angled forceps useful for reaching under vessels and tying knots.
- Modified jeweler's forceps with slender, polished tips used to dilate vessels.
- Titanium micro forceps (0.05 mm and 0.1 mm) are sufficient for most sutures.

## Vascular Clamps: Evolution and Design
- Evolved significantly since Jacobson's bulldog clamps.
- Ideally atraumatic with sufficient closing pressure to prevent bleeding.
- Divided into those used on veins or arteries.
- Vein clamps: Smaller closing pressure, flat jaw.
- Artery clamps: Greater closing pressure, slight incurve at tip.

## Vascular Clamps: Pressure and Sizing
- Available in a variety of sizes for different vessel diameters.
- Pressure is inversely proportional to vessel size.
- Ideal pressure: 5–10 g/mm² for largest vessels, 15–20 g/mm² for smallest.
- Use the smallest appropriate clamp to minimize crushing.
- Special applicators available for accurate placement.

## Vascular Clamps: Limitations and Alternatives
- Can cause intimal lesions, occupy space, and risk backwalling.
- Clampless anastomosis may be appealing.
- Thermo-sensitive gel (CE-certified) provides circular stenting and gentle distension.
- Dissolves completely with cold saline irrigation after anastomosis.
- Currently more common in cardiovascular surgery than microsurgery.

## Bipolar Coagulator
- Developed in 1956; promoted a completely bloodless field.
- Conducts current between the tips of jeweler's forceps.
- Heat damage limited to a very small area between tips.
- Allows precise coagulation of small branches as close as 2 mm to the main vessel.
- Power setting must be optimized to avoid spreading heat damage.

## Irrigation: Purpose and Methods
- Clear view of vessel walls is imperative.
- Constant irrigation with Ringer’s lactate or heparinized saline.
- Purposes:
  - Prevent desiccation of vessels
  - Prevent sticking of suture to tissue
  - Wash away blood, clots, and prothrombotic factors
- Performed via continuous system or a 5–10-mL syringe with a lacrimal cannula.

## Suction Techniques
- Small segments of moistened hydrocellulose sponge or gauze.
- Suction tubes draining through a perforated background plate.
- Homemade suction tips with an intravascular catheter attached to a 10 mL syringe.
- Cellulose spearheads (eye sponges) afford precise control for small oozes.

## Microsutures: History and Materials
- Buncke made his first microneedle by drilling a hole in a 75 mm stainless steel wire.
- Acland developed a commercially available needle.
- Available in combinations of materials, sizes (8-0 to 12-0), and needle configurations.
- Most widely used: Non-resorbable nylon (low tissue reactivity, good knot-holding).
- Polypropylene is preferred by some for better sliding within tissue.

## Microsutures: Sizing Guidelines
- 9-0: Vessels of 2 mm or more in diameter.
- 10-0: Vessels between 1 and 2 mm in diameter.
- 11-0 to 12-0: Smaller vessels (supramicrosurgery).
- Needle length: 5.1 mm preferred for 9-0 and 10-0; 3.6 mm for 11-0 and 12-0.
- Needles typically shaped as three-eighths of a circle, round, tapered tips.

## Anastomotic Devices: The Coupler System
- Developed to find faster, less traumatic anastomosis methods.
- Nakayama et al. (1962) introduced metallic rings with interlocking pins.
- UNILINK system (1986) led to the Microvascular Anastomotic COUPLER System.
- Consists of two disposable high-density polyethylene rings with stainless-steel pins.

## Coupler Devices: Advantages and Usage
- Simple, fast, and does not disturb the intima.
- Excellent patency rates (up to 100%), even in irradiated fields.
- Rings range from 1 to 4 mm, accommodating vessels from 0.8–4.3 mm.
- Suitable for both end-to-end and end-to-side anastomosis.
- Contraindicated in peripheral vascular disease, active infection, etc.

## Coupler Devices: Clinical Outcomes
- Venous anastomosis patency rates: 100% (coupler) vs. 95% (suture).
- Anastomotic time reduced to 2–6 minutes.
- Absorbable anastomotic couplers have been developed (absorbed at 70 days to 30 weeks).
- Mechanical coupling also successfully used in arterial anastomoses (up to 100% patency).
- Contraindications for arteries: thick-walled, >1.5:1 discrepancy, <1.5 mm diameter.

## Nonpenetrating Microvascular Stapler
- VCS clip applier system uses nonpenetrating titanium clips.
- Applied in an interrupted, everting fashion.
- Clips come in four sizes (0.9 to 3.0 mm).
- Reduces anastomotic time and maintains high patency rates.
- Requires stay sutures and an experienced assistant for proper eversion.

## Adhesives: Fibrin and Cyanoacrylate Glues
- Fibrin glues: Imitates the final pathway in coagulation.
- Reduces number of sutures and anastomotic time.
- Concerns: Glue entering vessel lumen, allergic reactions, anaphylaxis.
- Cyanoacrylates: Plagued by histotoxicity, foreign-body granulomatous response, and calcification.
- 2-Octyl-cyanoacrylate might be less toxic.

## Welding: Thermal and Laser Energy
- Thermal or laser welding extensively studied experimentally.
- Laser types: Nd:YAG, CO2, Argon, Diode.
- Show up to 100% patency rates and better blood flow in veins.
- Laser-activated protein solders introduced for strength.
- Clinical use limited by fear of weakening the anastomosis and pseudoaneurysm formation.

## Experimental Methods: Stents and Magnets
- Cylindrical or T-shaped intravascular stents.
- External metallic rings to keep cylindrical form and avoid through-stitching.
- Magnets tested in 1978; triggered to attract and compress arterial walls.
- Form a two-magnet vascular port for side-to-side AV or vein graft anastomoses.

## General Principles: Success Factors
- Success is multifactorial.
- Technical skills in vessel anastomosis are a must-have craft.
- Learning to perform 100%-patent microanastomoses is the first step.
- Requires a calm disposition, patience, and endurance.

## The Working Environment and Training
- Surgeon must concentrate without unnecessary interruptions.
- Competent assistant and specialized scrub nurse make a big difference.
- Training: Traditional apprenticeship model is insufficient.
- Special microsurgery fellowship is a must.
- Trainees can learn in clinical settings under supervision.

## Planning and Positioning
- Time spent planning and positioning is never wasted.
- Right position makes movements easier and procedure faster.
- Comfort relates directly to success.
- Two-team approach reduces operating time.
- Proper patient positioning alleviates need for repositioning.

## Surgeon and Microscope Positioning
- Surgeon seated comfortably, feet flat on the ground for a stable base.
- Forearms resting on folded drapes at the same level as the anastomosis.
- Minimizes tremor and fatigue.
- Microscope positioned to not obstruct movement but provide maximum control.
- Microscope base fixed to allow exact positioning.

## Securing the Flap or Flap Inset
- Inset considered before anastomosis is performed.
- After circulation restored, flap swells and bleeds, making inset difficult.
- Inset performed first ensures good hemostasis before pedicle division.
- Allows accurate judgment of pedicle length, avoiding tension or redundancy.

## Exceptions in Flap Inset
- Tailoring or thinning the flap is better performed while perfused.
- Allows better control of bleeders and avoids hematoma.
- Exception: Breast surgery where anastomosis lies deep to the inset.
- In such cases, flap is secured near the defect to allow adequate exposure.

## Selection of Recipient Vessels
- Use healthy vessels of appropriate size with good flow.
- Ideally away from zones of trauma, irradiation, inflammation, or scarring.
- Healthy vessel: Soft wall, vascular sheath easily dissected.
- Traumatized vessels: Encased in fibrotic tissue, prone to bleeding.

## Assessing Recipient Vessels
- Necessary to assess quality post-irradiation, in single-vessel legs, trauma, or diabetes.
- Recipient vessels do not have to be classic big vessels; perforating branches can be used.
- Veins are also considered and crucial in lymphatic reconstruction.
- Assessment via Doppler ultrasound, CTA, ICG imaging, or lymphoscintigraphy.

## Dissection of Recipient Vessels
- Done under loupes or microscope magnification.
- Free sufficient length for a tension-free anastomosis.
- Depends on flap pedicle length, depth of recipient vessels, and anastomosis technique.
- Deep vessels (e.g., internal thoracic) require greater dissection length to orient them superficially.

## Checking Vessel Quality and Flow
- Gross trimming of adventitia performed around the anastomosis area.
- Artery: Check for expansile pulsation and healthy spurting.
- If no spurt, check normotension, relieve vasospasm, or cut back to healthy tissue.
- Vein: Should be at least as wide as flap vein to avoid bottle-neck effect.
- Flush with heparinized saline to assess resistance and outflow.

## Preparation of Vessels: Inspection
- Lumens inspected for irregularities:
  - Intimal tears or separation
  - Thrombi
  - Atherosclerotic plaques
  - Friable calcified walls
- Debris gently irrigated away or removed with microforceps.
- Vessel cut back to attain a healthier segment if necessary.

## Vessel Wall Anatomy
- Tunica intima: Single layer of endothelium on basal lamina.
- Tunica media: Smooth-muscle cells, thickest layer in arteries, thinner in veins.
- Tunica adventitia: Loose areolar connective tissue containing vasa vasorum.
- Veins have the same layers but less defined, especially the tunica media.

## Adventitia Trimming and Dilatation
- Loose adventitia peeled off or sharply trimmed 3–4 mm from the anastomotic site.
- Prevents adventitia from falling into the lumen.
- Avoid overly aggressive stripping to prevent necrosis and false aneurysms.
- Lumens gently dilated in two planes with a vessel dilator.
- Aids suturing, prevents vasospasm, and flushes out blood.

- **Figure 25.1**: Horizontal vessel orientation allows adequate visualization of both lumens.
- **Figure 25.2**: Shows loose intima, separation of walls, and intraluminal valves/clots.
- **Figure 25.3**: Intraluminal irrigation of vessels to clear debris.

- **Figure 25.5**: Sharp trimming of adventitia parallel to the luminal edge.
- **Figure 25.6**: More radical resection of adventitia parallel to vessel length.
- **Figure 25.7**: Gentle luminal dilatation of the vessel end.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Artery First vs. Vein First
- No consensus on optimal sequence; dictated by ischemia time and vessel position.
- Arterial repair first: Shortens warm ischemia time.
- May reveal dominant venous drainage and detect pedicle twists.
- Disadvantage: Flap may bleed, affecting venous anastomosis and causing congestion.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Venous Drainage
- Venous anastomosis first: Allows better adjustment of pedicle length.
- Delays revascularization of the flap.
- Some advocate two venous anastomoses to avoid venous insufficiency.
- Single venous anastomosis is often adequate and reduces operative time.
- Sound judgment required based on flap anatomy and vein reliability.

## Anastomosis Techniques Overview
- End-to-end anastomosis is the most common method.
- Simple and appropriate for most arterial and venous anastomoses.
- Techniques include:
  - Halving
  - Triangulation
  - "Back wall-up"
- Principles: Avoid narrowing, avoid folds, oppose intimal edges closely.

## Interrupted Suturing: Stay Sutures
- Carrel recommended three stay sutures at 120° from each other.
- Cobbett modified to two stay sutures at 120°.
- Tensioning apart reduces chance of through-stitching the posterior wall.
- Alternative: Two stay sutures at 180° to ensure even spacing.

## Interrupted Suturing: Technique and Knot Tying
- Needle penetrates perpendicularly, incorporating all layers, especially intima.
- First throw is a double one to maintain tension, followed by two single throws.
- Knots snugged down by sight, not feel.
- Stop when edges meet and slightly evert.
- Too tight: Causes tears, subendothelium exposure, thrombosis, or media necrosis.

## Interrupted Suturing: Completing the Anastomosis
- Sutures placed between stay sutures.
- Aim for the smallest number of sutures for a leakproof anastomosis.
- Approximator clamp turned over to suture the back wall.
- Leave last few stitches untied until the last suture is placed to prevent through-stitching.

## Figures: Interrupted Suturing Techniques
- **Figure 25.9**: Interrupted suturing with stay sutures at 120° or 180°.
- **Figure 25.10**: Knot tying with a double throw.
- **Figure 25.11**: Placing a halving suture facilitates accurate stitch placement.
- **Figure 25.12**: Back wall first technique when clamp cannot be turned.

## Continuous Suturing: Advantages and Setup
- Suitable for minimally size-discrepant vessels >2 or 3 mm.
- Reduces anastomosis time by nearly half and is more hemostatic.
- Problems: Suture entanglement, risk of purse-string constriction.
- Place two or three stay sutures, leaving one end long.

## Continuous Suturing: Execution
- Running sutures placed at regular intervals and tied to the next stay suture.
- Needle passed under the vessel, double clamp turned over.
- Reduces likelihood of purse-string effect.
- Patency rates of 97.5–100% achievable with meticulous attention.

## Open-Loop Suturing
- Combines convenience of continuous with advantages of interrupted.
- Running suture performed leaving small loops.
- First suture tied and ends cut short.
- Next loop pulled through, tied, and cut.
- Reduces needle handling, maintains lumen visualization, eliminates purse-stringing.

## Sleeve Anastomosis
- Introduced by Lauritzen in 1978 ("end-in-end").
- Telescopes vessels using two extraluminal sutures.
- Fewer sutures required, reducing time and trauma.
- Low patency rates reported initially prevented popularity.
- Modification ("hemi-invagination") improved patency to 95–100% in rats.

## Figures: Continuous, Open-Loop, and Sleeve
- **Figure 25.13**: Continuous suture techniques preventing purse-stringing.
- **Figure 25.14**: Open-loop suture technique showing loop tying.
- **Figure 25.15**: Sleeve anastomosis telescoping one vessel inside the other.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Indications
- Useful for significant vessel size or wall thickness discrepancy.
- Need to preserve distal circulation (e.g., single-vessel leg).
- Anecdotally less prone to vessel spasm in lower extremities.
- Associated with higher success rates, though not necessarily higher patency than end-to-end.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Arteriotomy
- Arteriotomy or venotomy made in recipient vessel.
- Can be triangular, elliptical, or longitudinal slit.
- Hole should not have irregular edges.
- Acland–Banis arteriotomy clamp useful to pick up and excise an ellipse.
- Opening should not be longer than the diameter of the donor vessel.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Suturing Technique
- Sutures placed radially to the center of the arteriotomy.
- If flap vessel long enough, "front" wall completed before pulling vessel to suture "back" wall.
- If insufficient length, back wall must be performed first.
- Advantages: Higher success rate, greater freedom of planning, technical simplicity.

## Figures: End-to-Side Anastomosis
- **Figure 25.16**: Making the arteriotomy for end-to-side anastomosis.
- **Figure 25.17**: Suturing the back wall first when there is insufficient length to rotate the vessel.

## Using the Coupler Device
- Most common alternative to conventional suture.
- Time-saving with equivalent patency rates.
- Measure outer diameter of each vessel after gentle dilatation.
- In size-discrepant vessels, choose coupler matching the smaller vessel's outer diameter.

## Coupler Application Steps
- Load coupling device onto anastomotic instrument.
- Thread vessel end through ring and impale edges securely on pins.
- Impale on every other pin first for even spacing.
- Bring rings together by turning handle clockwise.
- Reinforce with hemostat forceps, then eject device by turning counterclockwise.

## Figure 25.18: Application of the Coupler Device
- **(A)**: Vessel oriented at 90° to applicator; vessel end impaled evenly on pins.
- **(B)**: Vessel anastomosed and released by turning the applicator handle.
- Ensures intimal eversion and minimal trauma.

## Size-Discrepant Vessels: Challenges
- Common despite careful planning.
- More problematic if inflow is big and flap artery small, or vice versa.
- Sudden change of caliber causes turbulence predisposing to thrombosis.
- Mismatches up to 4:1 can be anastomosed end-to-end depending on skill.

## Size-Discrepant Vessels: Techniques
- Gently stretch smaller vessel mechanically.
- Place interrupted sutures further apart on the larger vessel.
- Fish-mouth incision or oblique cut on smaller vessel (avoid >30° angle).
- If >3:1 discrepancy: Consider end-to-side, vein graft, or side branch.
- Last resort: Dilate smaller vessel maximally and taper larger vessel with a clip.

## Figure 25.19: Managing Size-Discrepant Vessels
- **(A)**: Smaller vessel end dilated, stretched, cut obliquely, or given a longitudinal side cut.
- **(B)**: Smaller vessel sutured as widely as possible to the larger vessel.
- A clip placed obliquely tapers the remaining end to reduce turbulence.

## Vertically Oriented Anastomosis
- Most challenging configuration of vessels.
- Change position of body part, surgeon, or table if possible.
- Free up more vessel length to manipulate into horizontal plane.
- If position cannot change, reduce microscope magnification.
- Increases depth of field, reducing need to constantly alter focus.

## Atherosclerosis and Loose Intima
- Common in elderly, cardiovascular disease, or post-radiotherapy.
- Significant plaque requires cutting back to healthier intima or choosing another vessel.
- Divide artery with sharp scissors in one cut to minimize intimal separation.
- Trim cut edge slowly and circumferentially.
- Avoid excessive microclamp tension to prevent fracturing calcified walls.

## Atherosclerosis: Suturing and Anastomosis Type
- Use a round needle and smallest microsuture.
- Pass suture from inside lumen to outside to avoid further intimal separation.
- Use counterpressure from forceps within the vessel.
- Avoid vessel dilatation; carefully evert vessel wall.
- End-to-end preferred over end-to-side to avoid direct plaque exposure.

## Figure 25.20: Counterpressure for Atherosclerosis
- Use of forceps to provide counterpressure to minimize trauma.
- Prevents separation of the intima from the vessel wall.
- Crucial when passing the needle through diseased, friable vessel walls.

## Microvascular Grafts: Indications and Harvest
- Diminished need due to proper planning, but sometimes necessary.
- Indications: Pedicle out of reach, tension, size mismatch, outside zone of injury.
- Harvest under loupe magnification.
- Graft should match caliber of vessels to be anastomosed.
- Great/lesser saphenous vein is the workhorse; upper limb veins for upper limb defects.

## Microvascular Grafts: Preparation and Direction
- Handle vein minimally; ligate all tributaries.
- Vein grafts contract after division but lengthen with high-pressure flow.
- Direction is crucial: Must have antegrade flow (proximal end marked with clip).
- Hydrodilatation stretches graft, untwists vein, and relieves vasospasm.
- Arterial grafts have advantages (no valves, anatomical taper) but no significant microvascular superiority.

## Testing Patency: Observation and Signs
- Assess after each anastomosis and periodically.
- Arterial pulsation: Expansile is good; longitudinal indicates thrombosis.
- Vein: Natural round diameter indicates patency.
- Engorged, dark blood column indicates thrombosis.
- Signs of non-patent vein: Engorgement of secondary veins, continuous dark bleeding from edges.

## Testing Patency: Physical Tests
- "Uplift" test: Gently hook up thin-walled vessel; alternate filling and collapsing with pulse indicates patency.
- Empty-and-refill test: Occlude vessel distal to anastomosis, empty a segment, release proximal occlusion.
- Immediate refill indicates patency; sluggish or absent refill indicates thrombosis.
- Use side branches for atraumatic assessment if preserved during dissection.

## Testing Patency: Modern Imaging
- ICG (Indocyanine green) imaging is much easier and more accurate.
- Many microscopes equipped with infrared cameras.
- Hand-held devices available to examine flap perfusion.
- Provides real-time, objective assessment of vascular flow and tissue viability.

## Figure 25.21: The Empty-and-Refill Test
- Slightly more traumatic; preferably performed on veins.
- Gently occlude vessel distal to anastomosis.
- Empty segment by running forceps in direction of flow.
- Release first pair of forceps; immediate refill confirms patency.

## General Aspects of Free Flap Surgery
- Evolved from replantation to complex tissue transfer.
- Success relies on:
  - Thorough preoperative planning
  - Flawless execution of anastomoses
  - Meticulous postoperative monitoring
- Clinical assessment remains the gold standard.
- Early detection of failing flap with prompt intervention improves salvage rates.

## Postoperative Care and Pharmacology
- Specialized microsurgical intensive care units improve outcomes.
- Pharmacological agents useful in specific scenarios:
  - Low-dose heparin
  - PGE1 (Prostaglandin E1)
  - Dextran
- Complications not only due to vascular compromise; inadequate planning or flawed execution also play roles.

## Re-exploration and Salvage Rates
- If first microsurgical reconstruction fails, a second can be attempted.
- Good results achievable after identifying and managing potential causes.
- Success rates of 96–98% in developed centers.
- Requires flexibility of the surgical plan and readiness to adapt.

## The Future of Microsurgery
- Microsurgery will not decline but continue to evolve.
- Revolutionized approach to reconstructive challenges.
- Wider applications expected in:
  - Supermicrosurgery (lymphatic, perforator-to-perforator)
  - Free-style free flaps
  - Composite tissue allotransplantation (hand, face)

## Advancements in Technology and Training
- Continued refinement of instruments and imaging (e.g., ICG, fluorescence).
- Development of new anastomotic devices and adhesives.
- Emphasis on specialized training and dedicated infrastructures.
- High-volume centers ensure convenience and consistently high success rates.

## Summary of Key Principles
- Magnification and illumination are fundamental.
- Atraumatic tissue handling and precise suturing are paramount.
- Healthy recipient vessels are essential for success.
- Tension-free anastomosis with good inflow and outflow.
- Meticulous postoperative monitoring ensures early intervention.

## Conclusion
- Microsurgery is mentally and physically demanding but highly rewarding.
- Combines art, science, and sophisticated technology.
- Continuous learning and specialization are required.
- Has transformed reconstructive surgery, offering superior functional and aesthetic outcomes.
- The future holds even more innovative applications and refinements.
